Orchot Tzadikim 21:13: The wise man said: whoever speaks with wisdom and good sense is like salt in the dish, and there is grace in the words of the discerning like a beryl set in gold. "The wisdom of the poor man is despised, and his words are not heeded" (Ecclesiastes 9:16) — let him go to a person whose words are heeded, and put his words in that person's mouth to make them heard; but he himself should remain silent.
Orchot Tzadikim 21:14: In sum: a person who makes a door for his entrance has a time to open it and a time to close it — so let him close the doors of his mouth with two doors: the lips and the teeth. And be very careful about opening your mouth, and guard your tongue, as you would guard silver, gold, and pearls in your room and inside your chests, making a lock upon a lock — so do with your mouth. See how the early ones were careful about idle talk all their days. And in this matter there is a great remedy for praying with intent, for most of the loss of intent in prayer comes from idle words fixed in one's heart. Silence is also a great fence for the fear of Heaven, for it is impossible for fear of Heaven to be in the heart of one who talks excessively.
Orchot Tzadikim 21:15: Now I must explain to you four gates concerning four groups that do not receive the presence of the Divine Presence (Sotah 42a): the group of scoffers, as it is written (Hosea 7:5), "he stretched out his hand with scoffers"; the group of liars, as it is written (Psalms 101:7), "he who speaks falsehood shall not be established before my eyes"; the group of flatterers, as it is written (Job 13:16), "for a flatterer shall not come before Him"; the group of slanderers, as it is written (Psalms 5:5), "for You are not a God who desires wickedness; evil shall not sojourn with You." And now I must give you insight into their dealings and divide their categories, for there is much benefit in understanding the matter fully.
Orchot Tzadikim 21:16: Mockery divides into five parts. The first: a man who casts blame upon people, as it is said (Psalms 50:20), "you sit and speak against your brother; you slander your own mother's son." And whoever does this is called a "scoffer," as it is written (Proverbs 21:24), "haughty, insolent, scoffer is his name, he acts in the fury of insolence." The meaning of the verse is this: "haughty, insolent, scoffer" — mockery contains two bad traits: one, that he acts deliberately, committing the transgression willfully, doing his fellow harm and great loss in a matter from which he gains nothing. For when he casts blame and makes his fellow's reputation stink in people's eyes, making him hated — this is the ultimate deliberateness, more than a thief or robber. For when he steals or robs, it is not out of deliberate malice, but for his own benefit, to increase his wealth; but one who casts blame upon people gains nothing from it, and it is a defect of the heart. And the scoffer is also haughty, full of pride, and this is why he casts blame upon people. But the wise man, being humble and lowly, recognizes his own faults, and therefore does not mock people to cast blame on them, in the manner of scoffers who sit and say "so-and-so did such-and-such" and mock him.
Orchot Tzadikim 21:17: The second: one who mocks people's words because he despises them, since they too have not succeeded in wealth and honor; and he mocks the poor, not casting a blemish on them, but they are simply despicable in his eyes. And this matter comes from pride, or sometimes it comes from ease and abundance of pleasure, as it is said (Psalms 123:4), "our soul has had more than enough of the scorn of those at ease." This is proof that those at ease are the mockers, and sometimes, in the abundance of their ease, they mock the righteous, as it is said (Jeremiah 20:7), "everyone mocks me." And it is said (Proverbs 17:5), "whoever mocks the poor reproaches his Maker" — its meaning: whoever mocks a poor man because he is poor, and it seems in his eyes that his being poor is because of his lack of wisdom, and that his own being rich is because of his own wisdom, as it is said (Deuteronomy 8:17), "my own power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth" — this mocking man reproaches the Blessed Creator, for is not the poor man too the work of the Blessed Lord, as it is written (Proverbs 22:2), "the rich and the poor meet together; the Lord is the Maker of them all" — behold, he is mocking the work of the Blessed Lord.
Orchot Tzadikim 21:18: The third: there is one who mocks matters without intending to disgrace those who did them, but rather distances himself from undertakings that have hope and a future outcome to their work. And this scoffer is wise in his own eyes, and every deed he himself has not begun seems to him foolish, and he mocks it. And sometimes this trait brings him to heresy, mocking the commandments, as it is written (Psalms 119:51), "the proud have utterly derided me, yet I have not turned aside from Your law." And this scoffer does not accept rebuke, as it is said (Proverbs 9:8), "do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you"; and it says (ibid. verse 7), "he who corrects a scoffer gets shame for himself." And because he is wise in his own eyes, he mocks the work of another person. And this is the trait for which there is no hope, as it is said (ibid. 26:12), "you see a man wise in his own eyes — there is more hope for a fool than for him."
Orchot Tzadikim 21:19: The fourth: one who fixes himself constantly to idle talk and vain words, like those who sit at street corners. And they search with all their ability to find mockery, for they have no other occupation than sitting and mocking people and jeering at their deeds. And there are two evils in this: one, that whoever talks excessively brings on sin; the second, that he becomes idle from the words of Torah. And there are ways of death in this matter, for he does not take to heart that at this very time he sits mocking, he could have been studying or performing a commandment, to acquire the life of the World to Come.
Orchot Tzadikim 21:20: The fifth: one who mocks a deed or words, not because he despises the deed he mocks, but he mocks in the manner of those who play, by way of jest. And sometimes this is caused by drinking wine, as it is said (Proverbs 20:1), "wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler."
Orchot Tzadikim 21:21: And know that mockery does not become a fixed habit in a person until he has already thrown off the yoke of Heaven from himself. Therefore he brings punishment upon himself, to be given sufferings, measure for measure, as it is said (Isaiah 28:22), "now therefore be not scoffers, lest your bonds be made strong." And the Sages would warn their students not to mock even by way of accident or chance occurrence (Avodah Zarah 18b). They needed to warn their students of this because many stumble into mockery by way of chance occurrence. Whoever mocks those who perform the commandments — this matter tends toward heresy, for it means he does not believe in the commandments. And this is like one who mocks the king's command — does such a one have any life at all?! And further: this mocker causes others to sin, in that they too will not perform the commandments, for the one who performs the commandment will become lax in it, and others too will not perform the commandment, because they fear the mockers. But regarding idolatry, one may mock it (Sanhedrin 63b). And one may mock those who commit transgressions, in order to keep them from the transgression, and so that others too, seeing them mocked, will not commit transgressions.
Orchot Tzadikim 22:2: Falsehood. Know that just as a person weighs silver and gold on a scale, distinguishing between light and heavy, so the wise person weighs on a scale to understand falsehood and truth. And there is a difference between one falsehood and another. How so? One who says of wood that it is gold — that falsehood is obvious. One who says of blank copper that it is gold — that falsehood requires discernment, for the two have the same appearance, and there are counterfeiters who make copper look like gold; and then even experts can distinguish only with great difficulty. So it is with the matter of thought: there is one who is sophisticated and constructs arguments to uphold falsehood, until it appears to be truth. But the wise man understands each one, distinguishing between falsehood and truth. And this is a matter known to all: that falsehood and truth are compressed together in a single heart. There is a counterfeit person who, even though he knows for certain that a thing is false, is drawn after it — how much more so when there are arguments on the side of the falsehood, making it seem to be true, that he will surely be drawn after his falsehood. But there is a truthful person, who will not act falsely except when there are arguments for him to lie — then he is drawn after the falsehood. And the wise man will refute the false arguments with his wisdom. And you must know that every person is drawn after his own reasonings and his own traits: the lazy man will make all his reasonings follow laziness, and likewise the angry man follows his anger, and likewise the proud man follows his pride. And so with all the traits we have explained — according to the trait a person has, so he acts: the squanderer follows squandering, the stingy man follows stinginess, the lover follows his love, the hater follows his hatred. Therefore a person who wishes to be a true man of God must first remove from himself all the bad traits, so that the trait within him not draw him according to its own nature. And then he will be able to attain the truth.
Orchot Tzadikim 22:3: There are nine categories in the matter of falsehood. The first: one who denies his fellow regarding a deposit or a loan, or gives false testimony, and many similar things. And there are two punishments for this falsehood: one because of the falsehood itself, for falsehood, even without harm, is an abomination to the Blessed Lord, as it is said (Proverbs 6:16-19), "these six things the Lord hates, and seven are an abomination to His soul: haughty eyes, a lying tongue... a false witness who breathes out lies, and one who sows discord among brothers." And it says (ibid. 8:13), "and a perverse mouth I hate." The second punishment is because of the harm he did to his fellow.
Orchot Tzadikim 22:4: The second: there is no direct harm to his fellow in the falsehood itself, but he intends to deceive his fellow into believing him and trusting him and not guarding against him — and then he will be able to harm him, as it is said (Jeremiah 9:7), "with his mouth one speaks peaceably to his neighbor, but in his heart he lies in wait." And even in the eyes of flesh and blood falsehood is despised, as it is said (Proverbs 16:12-13), "it is an abomination for kings to commit wickedness... righteous lips are the delight of kings."
Orchot Tzadikim 22:5: The third: one who lies to his fellow not to rob him of anything of his own, but he sees a good thing that is destined to come to his fellow, and he pursues that good thing to take it for himself through falsehood and deceit. Or he speaks falsehoods to his fellow until the fellow gives him a gift — such as bringing him false good news so he gives him gifts for it, and the like of this matter. And our Sages of blessed memory said (Sanhedrin 92a): whoever changes his word is as though he worshipped idols, as it is said (Genesis 27:12), "perhaps my father will feel me, and I shall be as a deceiver in his eyes"; and of idolatry it is said (Jeremiah 10:15), "they are vanity, the work of deception (ta'atu'im)." And it does not mean "as though he actually worshipped idols" but by a certain resemblance: for he hides himself in falsehood and is aided by vanity.
Orchot Tzadikim 22:6: The fourth: one who lies in relating things he heard, changing part of them intentionally; and he gains no benefit at all from that falsehood, nor does it harm his fellow. And sometimes he relates things he has fabricated entirely from his own mind. And he has a punishment, for he loves falsehood without benefit. And of this Solomon, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 6:19), "a false witness who breathes out lies." And you must know that this trait will bring him to give false testimony against his own brother, because he loves falsehood. And there are people who change part of what they heard unknowingly, because they do not take it to heart, at the time they hear things, to investigate their truth — this too is a bad trait, and of this Solomon, peace upon him, said (ibid. 21:28), "but the man who listens [attentively] shall speak forever"; its meaning: whoever takes care to listen and understand the content of the matter and the words that are related, because they related them in a truthful way, so that no false speech is found in his mouth — that man shall speak forever, for people will desire to hear his words, and will not rebuke him for what he says.
Orchot Tzadikim 22:7: The fifth: one who tells his fellow that he will do him good, or give him a gift, or help him, and does not tell him this in a manner of firm commitment for his fellow's heart to rely on, while at the very moment he says this, it was in his heart not to give it. Of this our Sages said (Bava Metzia 49a) that one's mouth and heart should not differ.
Orchot Tzadikim 22:8: The sixth: one who promises his fellow to do him good, and promises so firmly that his fellow's heart relies on it — he must not violate his promise. And if he lies about this, his punishment is greater than the previous case, which was mere words alone. And one who tells his fellow he will give him a small gift, even though he did not use words of firm promise, we say (ibid.) that whoever retracts his word is suspected of untrustworthiness, for his fellow's heart relies and trusts him, since the gift is small.
Orchot Tzadikim 22:9: And if he is a poor man, even though the gift is large, if he retracts, his wickedness is great, for he has vowed and transgressed "he shall not violate his word" (Numbers 30:3). And likewise one who boasted before many people that he would give a gift to someone — this is like a firm promise, since he glorifies himself over his own generosity, and it is not proper for him to retract his words after he has been honored and glorified by the matter.
Orchot Tzadikim 22:10: The seventh: one who deceives his fellow into saying that he did him a kindness, or spoke well of him, when he did not. Of this our Sages of blessed memory said (Chullin 94a): it is forbidden to steal people's minds, even the mind of a gentile. And there is sin in this, for we are obligated to speak words of truth, since it is among the foundations of the soul.
Orchot Tzadikim 22:11: The eighth: one who boasts of virtues he does not actually possess, and this is a great sin even if it were true. For when he praises himself, it appears from his words that he did his charitable and generous deeds not for the sake of Heaven but for his own sake and for praise. And our Sages of blessed memory said (Yerushalmi Shevi'it 10:5): whoever is honored by people who suppose he knows two tractates, when he knows only one, is obligated to tell them, "I know only one." How much more so is it forbidden for him to lie and boast of virtues he does not have.
Orchot Tzadikim 22:12: The ninth: one who, in relating things he has heard, changes matters concerning his own affairs, without causing loss to any person, but derives a small pleasure from his falsehood, even though he gains no money from it. For instance (Yevamot 63a), Rav, who said to his wife: "make me lentils," and she made him chickpeas, and when he said "chickpeas" she made him lentils. His son Chiya went and reversed matters: when he wanted chickpeas, he told his mother, "make lentils," and she made chickpeas. And this son did this in honor of his father, so that the food his father wanted would be ready for him; nonetheless he was rebuked for doing this again, because of "they have taught their tongue to speak falsehood" (Jeremiah 9:4). But there is no punishment in this falsehood equal to the punishment of those who lie for no reason at all, as we mentioned in the fourth category.
Orchot Tzadikim 22:13: Thus far the nine categories of falsehood. Further, a person must be careful: if his fellow comes to him and asks for something he has in hand, he should not tell him, "I do not have it," but should turn him away in a manner that involves no falsehood. And there is a ruling in Sefer Chasidim (section 426): even if a gentile comes to a Jew's house and asks to borrow money, and the Jew has money but does not wish to lend it to this gentile, he should not tell him, "I do not have it," but should turn him away however he can without falsehoods. And it is possible that if the gentile knew that had the Jew had money he could not have avoided [lending] without incurring hatred, it would be better to say "I do not have it," for the sake of peaceful relations. But everything depends on the person's own judgment, on how the gentile's situation appears to him: if he can say, "I have it, but I need it for something else," and by this can turn him away without incurring hatred, he should do so.
Orchot Tzadikim 22:14: And great is the punishment of a liar: even when he speaks the truth, he is not believed (Sanhedrin 89b). And falsehood has no legs [to stand on] (beginning of Otiyot d'Rabbi Akiva).
Orchot Tzadikim 22:15: And a person should not cause others to lie on his behalf. How so? When a person sees two people speaking together some private matter between them, he should not go to one of them and ask him to reveal the matter, for perhaps he does not wish to reveal it, and through this will put him off with other words — meaning he will be caused to lie. And so he should be exacting in all his affairs, that he not lie in his business dealings, and not cause others to lie. And he should be careful not to associate with liars, and minimize his words with them. And great wisdom is needed to be saved from falsehood, for the evil inclination always lies in wait for a person to catch him in its net.
Orchot Tzadikim 22:16: And sometimes the Sages permitted lying, such as to make peace between a person and his fellow (Yevamot 65b). And likewise it is permitted to praise a bride before the groom as beautiful and graceful, even though she is not (Ketubot 17a). And regarding lodging: if the host did him good, he should not say before many people, "how good is so-and-so, that I lodged in his house! What great honor he did me!" — lest many unworthy people come to lodge with him. Of this it is said (Proverbs 27:14), "he who blesses his friend with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted a curse to him" (Arachin 16a).
Orchot Tzadikim 22:17: And regarding a tractate: if asked whether he has it fluent on his tongue, it is a trait of humility to say "no." And regarding the marital bed: if he was delayed in coming to synagogue because he had marital relations, and was asked why he was delayed, he should attribute it to other matters (Bava Metzia 23b). And in all these cases where the Sages permitted altering the truth, if he can manage without lying at all, it is better than lying. For instance, if he is asked, "do you know such-and-such a tractate?" he could answer, "and do you suppose that I know it?!" And if he can turn away the questioner in a way that involves no falsehood, this is very good.
Orchot Tzadikim 23:2: Truth. The soul is created from the place of the Holy Spirit, as it is said (Genesis 2:7), "and He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life"; and it was hewn from a place of purity, and created from the supernal splendor of the Throne of Glory. And above, in the place of the Holy of Holies, there is no falsehood, but everything is truth, as it is said (Jeremiah 10:10), "but the Lord God is truth." And I found that it is written, "I will be that I will be" (Exodus 3:14), and it is written, "but the Lord God is truth; He is the living God and the everlasting King" (Jeremiah, ibid.).
Orchot Tzadikim 23:3: And now I must make known to you that the Holy One, blessed be He, is the God of truth: for you will find twenty-one occurrences of "ehyeh" [I will be], which is the numerical value of "emet" [truth], and likewise "ehyeh" itself has the numerical value of twenty-one.
Orchot Tzadikim 23:4: And God made man to be upright (Ecclesiastes 7:29), and the seal of the Holy One, blessed be He, is truth (Shabbat 55a). And it is written, "he who speaks falsehood shall not be established before my eyes" (Psalms 101:7). And when a person deals in falsehood, then falsehood does not cling to truth. And when there is truth, His seat is, as it were, established in heaven with regard to people, for when there is truth among people, they then acknowledge that He made heaven and earth, and the sea, and all that is in them. And this is what is said (Psalms 146:6), "who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them," and adjacent to it, "who keeps truth forever, who executes justice..." And when there is treachery and falsehood, then, as it were, His seat is not established in heaven or on earth. And whoever merits to reflect on these matters, how souls are hewn from the source of truth, will conduct all his affairs in truth, and will not bring falsehood into the place of the holiness of truth. And therefore the verse says (Psalms 145:18), "the Lord is near to all who call upon Him, to all who call upon Him in truth," for the Holy One, blessed be He, who is truth, draws near to whoever calls upon Him in truth. And what is called "a true calling"? This is one who clears his heart of everything in the world, and draws near to the Holy One, blessed be He, alone, and his intellect grows and strengthens to cleave to the supernal light, and he sets his thought upon his longing for Him always. And a person attains this matter when he is secluded in his room. And for this reason every pious man greatly increases separation and seclusion, and does not associate with people except for great need. But if he prays with the motion of his lips toward the wall while thinking of worldly matters, reciting with his tongue while his heart is elsewhere — whether thinking of glorifying himself for how pleasant his voice is, in order to find favor in people's eyes and receive praise from them — then his service is not truthful. And he is among those of whom it is said (Jeremiah 12:2), "You are near in their mouth, but far from their innermost being."
Orchot Tzadikim 23:5: Therefore we pray: "and purify our hearts to serve You in truth" — that we perform all our service in truthfulness, and believe with heart and willing soul, and not for the sake of people, and not for money or vain desire. And this is what is said (Job 22:23), "if you return to the Almighty, you shall be built up" — that no [alien] thought interposes between you and the Almighty, then you shall be built up with a strong structure in the splendor of the Divine Presence. Therefore David said (Psalms 15:1-2), "Lord, who shall sojourn in Your tent? Who shall dwell in Your holy mountain? He who walks uprightly, and does what is right, and speaks truth in his heart" — and it does not say "speaks truth with his mouth," but rather means that truth should be fixed and firmly established in a person's heart. Therefore the early pious ones, when they had a sale, would give it to the buyer according to what their hearts had resolved upon, however they had agreed to give it, even if the buyer wished to add more — they wanted only what their hearts had resolved upon. An important person who walks this path, to speak truth in his heart, if he resolved in his thoughts to do a certain thing, should write down that thought, so that he not forget it and not violate the words of his own resolutions. And if he cannot stand by it, let him go to a sage and have him release him from his resolutions. And let him take care that there be nothing in his thoughts as long as he has not yet uttered them with his mouth.
Orchot Tzadikim 23:6: Whoever speaks truth in his heart, and does not wish to think falsehood, even in matters he does not intend seriously — all his words and thoughts will be fulfilled, as it is said (Job 22:28), "you shall decree a thing, and it shall be established for you." And whoever is a man of truth, in all his business dealings, whether in buying and selling or in lending — he should always state his final intent at the outset, and accustom all those who deal with him to know that he will not change it, neither add to it nor subtract from it. The wise man said: always set truth before you. His intent is that one should make signs for himself. For instance, to remember not to lie in his business dealings, he should write it down, and keep that writing with him, and look at it before his dealings. And likewise he should write in his study hall and on his table, so that he remember not to speak falsehood, and so that he not forget to speak the truth. And so did one sage: he wrote on the walls of his house and in his study hall, on all the walls, up above: "remember the day of death and you will not sin." And whoever speaks only truth will live, lengthen his days, and be saved.
Orchot Tzadikim 23:7: Support for this matter is what the verse says (Jeremiah 10:10), "but the Lord God is truth; He is the living God and the everlasting King." And if one speaks only truth, he will be saved all the days of his life, as it is written (Malachi 2:6-7), "the law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found on his lips... for he is the messenger of the Lord of Hosts." The supernal angels are of the form of truth and are not in bodies, and souls shine from them like the light coming from the sun. Souls are in bodies, and therefore they know hidden things only a little, and in the visions of the night, for it is then that souls are not occupied with the needs of the body, and whoever knows the secret of souls will attest to this matter. And dreams are akin to thoughts, as it is written (Daniel 2:29), "your thoughts came to you upon your bed." And dreams come by way of the angel that accompanies a person. And since not all thoughts are true, therefore not all dreams are true. And whoever accustoms himself to have all his thoughts be true will also, at night, see true visions, and will know future things like the angels.
Orchot Tzadikim 23:8: And there is no virtue like speaking truth. And so it is written (Psalms 119:160), "the sum of Your word is truth"; and it is said (Exodus 23:7), "keep far from a false matter."
Orchot Tzadikim 23:9: Also, a person's hints and gestures should be truthful, for the reward of truth is very great; therefore let him accustom himself to walk in truth. And let him study Torah and know the truth, so that he can perform the commandments in their true and proper form. And let him always acknowledge the truth. Even in matters of aggadah that have no bearing on the fulfillment of commandments, let him study, so that his heart come to believe true things. And do not be ashamed to accept the truth from whoever it may be, even from the smallest and most despised of the small — even so, accept the truth from him. For a fine pearl in the hand of a small and despised person is nonetheless still a precious pearl.
Orchot Tzadikim 23:10: And now that the exile has lasted, because of our many sins, far too long, Israel must separate itself from the vanities of the world and hold fast to the seal of the Holy One, blessed be He, which is truth, and sanctify themselves even in what is permitted to them (Yevamot 20a), and not lie to a fellow Jew or to a gentile, and not deceive them in any matter, as it is said (Zephaniah 3:13), "the remnant of Israel shall do no wrong, nor speak lies, nor shall a deceitful tongue be found in their mouth." And it is further written (Hosea 2:25), "and I will sow her for Myself in the land" — does a person sow a single kor of seed only to bring in a single kor? So the Holy One, blessed be He, sowed Israel among the lands, so that converts would be added to them (Pesachim 87b), and as long as they conduct themselves without deceit, converts will cling to them. And behold, the Holy One, blessed be He, was strict about the robbery of the wicked, as it is said (Genesis 6:11), "and the earth was filled with violence."
Orchot Tzadikim 23:11: There is a story of Rabbi Shimon ben Shatach, who bought a donkey from a certain Ishmaelite. His students went and found a precious stone hanging around its neck. His students said to him: Rabbi, "the blessing of the Lord makes rich" (Proverbs 10:22). He said to them: I bought a donkey, I did not buy a precious stone. He went and returned it to that Ishmaelite. That Ishmaelite exclaimed over him: Blessed be the God of Shimon ben Shatach! (Devarim Rabbah 3:3). And so it is found in the Yerushalmi (Yerushalmi Bava Metzia 2:5): elder sages bought wheat from gentiles, and found in it a bundle of coins, and returned it to them. The gentiles said: blessed is the God of the Jews! And there are many such stories of returning items for the sake of the sanctification of the Name.
Orchot Tzadikim 23:12: And when there is truth below, then the Blessed Lord looks down in righteousness upon the earth, as it is said (Psalms 85:12), "truth shall spring up from the earth, and righteousness shall look down from heaven." Therefore see that all your affairs be in truth, whether for bad or for good, and rely upon the Faithful God, "who keeps covenant and kindness to those who love Him and keep His commandments" (Deuteronomy 7:9).
Orchot Tzadikim 23:13: And what is His faithfulness? That He keeps the covenant. If a righteous man commits a light sin, He collects the payment for it in this world. And this is a clear matter: it is better for the righteous man to be judged even with sufferings like Job all the days of his body — which is a lowly thing, in this world, where he has only a short time to live — and to receive good reward for his soul, which is honored in the supernal world, where it neither perishes nor ceases forever — and this is better for the righteous man than if his sins were not collected from him in this world, and he were instead judged in the world of souls with the sufferings of Gehinnom; or that, because of his sin, his soul's rank in the world of souls be diminished, and its cleaving to the supernal splendor, whose light has no comparison or parallel. And to the wicked He gives their reward in a brief pleasure that ceases in this brief world, while their sin is preserved for the long world, and for great suffering, which is Gehinnom, a suffering beyond compare.
Orchot Tzadikim 23:14: May the Merciful One guide us in His truth, and bring us into His chambers to reach the supernal light, where His mighty concealment and the splendor of His glory abide.
